_comment: Pinned engine bundle the Scan Pack router orchestrates (S3). Every engine emits native SARIF that build_sarif.py merges via _enrich_run. version_pin is the tested version. install_engines.sh downloads these into scan_pack/bin/ (verified against the upstream release checksums); scan_pack.py prefers scan_pack/bin/ over PATH. Add an engine here, not in code.

engines._metrics_comment: --metrics off is legal ONLY because --config points at a pinned local snapshot. It is invalid with --config auto: semgrep exits 2 with 'Cannot create auto config when metrics are off', because auto sets is_using_registry=True and that registry call IS the metrics call. If you ever revert to auto, remove this flag in the same change. {rules} is substituted by scan_pack.py, which falls back to auto (and says so in the coverage block) when the snapshot is absent.
engines.name: semgrep
engines._comment: One run writes BOTH formats. The SARIF is kept exactly as Semgrep wrote it; the JSON copy ({out}.semgrep.json) is the only place Semgrep reports each rule's confidence, impact, likelihood and subcategory as typed fields, so post_process copies those four onto each SARIF result's properties.torana. The SARIF alone carries confidence only as a free-text tag and the other three not at all.

engines.name: trivy-fs
engines._comment: Dependency (SCA) scanning from the repo's own manifests and lock files. Emits Trivy's NATIVE JSON, converted by post_process -- same reason as trivy-image: Trivy's own SARIF puts package identity in prose. PREFERRED OVER OSV where the binary resolves, because Trivy parses the manifests ITSELF. The OSV route takes a package list assembled by hand (SKILL.md Step 2 shows a literal echo), so which manifest gets trusted is a judgement call made per run -- on a typical service that is a few hundred pinned packages in requirements.txt versus 43 in pyproject.toml. Same inputs, different answers. Trivy removes that step.
engines._file_patterns_comment: ⛔ TRIVY PICKS ITS PARSER BY FILENAME, and only `requirements.txt` matches pip. A lock file named anything else is never opened -- not even if you point trivy straight at it (`trivy fs .../requirements_lock.txt` returns Results: None, because the filename still drives parser selection). MEASURED on Classie: classie-tenant-manager stored 0 dependency findings while its only real dependency description, requirements/requirements_lock.txt (38 pins), went unread -- and a 0 nobody can distinguish from 'we did not look' cannot be ranked on. classie_backend has three more of the same shape (core/ 126, eval/ 101, ask_classie/ 57 pins). --file-patterns declares them in place: no staged copies, no renaming. The second pattern (v2.8.3) is the pip-compile / `uv pip compile -o requirements.lock` convention: a base image's requirements.lock (and every repo shaped like it) got NO dependency scan before it -- measured with `trivy fs --format cyclonedx` on that lock, 0 packages under the old pattern alone and every pin under both, including the `pkg==v \ --hash=` continuation form. Widen the regex when a new naming convention shows up; the long-term fix is to DISCOVER manifests in the repo and declare them, rather than relying on Trivy to find them.

engines.name: trivy-image
engines._comment: Emits Trivy's NATIVE JSON, not its SARIF, and post_process converts it. Trivy's own SARIF puts package identity in prose and has no field for fix status: measured on one image, ingesting it landed cve_id 0/366 and package_name 0/366, so the findings could not join a pkg: node. trivy_to_sarif.py reads the typed JSON fields instead and emits the Torana profile.

_deep_tier_comment: SC2 opt-in deep tier. NOT in `engines[]` on purpose — scan_pack.py's generic router never runs these; they are driven by their `runner` (vvah_run.py). install_engines.sh DOES provision them (method `source` = git clone + pip install into the isolated venv). VVAH has no releases/tags yet, so version_pin is the exact main-branch commit (git ls-remote, 2026-07-07) for reproducibility; bump it deliberately.
_libraries_comment: Python LIBRARIES a reference script imports in-process. NOT engines[]: nothing execs them, they emit no SARIF, and scan_pack.py's router would try to run one as a command. install_engines.sh installs them into the SAME isolated venv as the pip engines and symlinks no binary; the importing script adds that venv's site-packages for its own interpreter (reachability_pass.py::python_parser). They install on a bare run, like the fast-tier engines, because a customer's CI runs install_engines.sh with no arguments — an opt-in library would mean every CI code-reachability answer is `inconclusive`.

libraries.name: tree-sitter
libraries.used_by: references/reachability_pass.py — the call graph behind a code finding's reachability verdict
libraries._comment: The core wheel plus ONE grammar per language the call graph parses (this entry carries Python; the tree-sitter-javascript and tree-sitter-typescript entries below carry the rest), not tree-sitter-language-pack (1.22.1), which bundles grammars for dozens of languages this pass never parses. The pass still falls back to the pack when a runner already has it. ⚠️ Every grammar entry repins `tree-sitter` itself, identically, so `--engines <one grammar>` installs a working parser on its own; pip resolves the repeated pin to the same wheel. ⚠️ The PACKAGE half of the reachability queue needs none of this — it is an import scan over the tree — so a runner without this library still answers the majority of the work list, and says why it cannot answer the rest.

libraries.name: tree-sitter-javascript
libraries.used_by: references/reachability_pass.py — the npm half of the call graph, which the API-diff check reads to decide whether this tree uses a changed npm symbol
libraries._comment: Covers .js, .jsx, .mjs and .cjs (the grammar parses JSX). Without it the npm API-diff check has no call graph and falls back to a whole-tree word match, which cannot tell a use of the changed symbol from the same word in a comment. ⚠️ A call graph for these files answers a JavaScript code finding's reachability only where the tree's entry points can be ENUMERATED: `entry` records are emitted for the frameworks the library enumerates (Express today), and a tree declaring an entry-defining package it does not enumerate comes back `inconclusive` naming that package rather than `no_path_from_entry_point`. Judged against the packages the tree DECLARES, so it fails closed: a partial entry set would turn an unenumerated route into a confident false negative.

libraries.name: tree-sitter-typescript
libraries.used_by: references/reachability_pass.py — the .ts and .tsx half of the npm call graph, same reader as tree-sitter-javascript
libraries._comment: Pinned a minor behind the other two because 0.23.2 is the latest release of this wheel — the three grammars version independently, which is why each is its own entry with its own version_pin. Verified loading against tree-sitter 0.26.0. ⚠️ ONE wheel, TWO languages: `language_typescript()` for .ts and `language_tsx()` for .tsx. They are different parsers and a .tsx file read with the .ts one does not parse, so a caller must pick by extension, not per wheel.

libraries.name: libcst
libraries.used_by: references/codemod_python.py — the 4a/4b codemods (phase 5); a CONCRETE syntax tree, so a rewrite keeps comments, blank lines and quote style and the diff shows only the line that changed
libraries._comment: ⛔ Installed with --require-hashes from libcst-requirements.txt (G2: fetched at install, pinned, hash-checked; never vendored per platform). --no-deps: the codemod path never imports yaml (prototype § 2). One wheel per (platform, Python minor); a cell with no wheel (Intel macOS, Windows) fails the import test and the codemod reports libcst_unavailable — a decline, never a guess. ⚠️ `import libcst` IS the test, not the pip exit code: the failure the prototype measured was exactly `cannot import name 'native'` from a zipimport, which installs cleanly.

rulesets.name: semgrep-default
rulesets._comment: The ruleset --config auto serves, fetched ONCE at install and frozen, instead of re-fetched on every scan. auto is NOT repo-aware: config_resolver.py builds the bare URL 'https://semgrep.dev/c/auto' with no project parameter, and that 302-redirects to '/c/p/default' -- the same 1074 rules for everyone. Rule-to-file selection happens LOCALLY by the languages: field. So there is no per-repo behaviour to reproduce here; pinning the snapshot reproduces auto exactly.
rulesets._why_comment: Three things auto costs. (1) A finding-count delta cannot be attributed: the ruleset can change under you and nothing in the SARIF records which one ran, so code changes and rule changes are indistinguishable after the fact. (2) Telemetry is inseparable -- config_resolver sets is_using_registry=True for auto, which forces the metrics POST to metrics.semgrep.dev, and semgrep exits 2 if you pass --metrics off anyway. (3) Every scan needs semgrep.dev reachable. Snapshotting fixes all three at once.
rulesets._fidelity_comment: ⚠️ This endpoint is NOT versioned -- there is no way to request 'p/default as of 2026-03'; you pin whatever it serves on install day. It also returns the SAME rules in a DIFFERENT ORDER on each fetch (measured 30 min apart: identical 1074 rule ids, identical 2423491 bytes, 3704 lines of diff, same digest once sorted), so NO content hash is recorded -- a raw one would report drift on every re-provision when nothing changed. install_engines.sh records source + fetched_at; scan_pack.py stamps ruleset_status/_source/_fetched_at into run.properties.torana.coverage. Re-run install_engines.sh to move the pin.
